food.text: The Forme of Cury, written around 1390 in the reign of King Richard II, shows that medieval English cooking was far from plain. It offers imaginative recipes using nutmeg, ginger, cinnamon, cardamon and cloves, with spicy sweet and sour sauces thickened with bread or ground almonds.

In France, livestock were slaughtered at the beginning of winter, and the meat was preserved for the cold months. Beef was often salted, while pork was salted and smoked. Bacon and sausages were smoked in the chimney, and tongue and hams were brined and dried.

In the north, including the British Isles and northern France, the climate was generally too harsh for growing grapes and olives. Beer was the commoner's drink there, while wine was an expensive import. Olive oil also stayed costly, so oil of poppy, walnut, hazel and filbert was the most affordable alternative.

Clarissa Dickson Wright rejects the popular idea that medieval cooks used spices to disguise bad meat, since spoiled meat would have been as fatal then as now. She suggests spices were instead used to hide the taste of salt, which preserved food in the absence of refrigeration.

Because whale, dolphin and porpoise were considered fish, the salted meats of these sea mammals were eaten in medieval France during Lent. The ingredients of the time varied greatly according to the seasons and the church calendar.

Poume d'oranges was a gilded pork meatball dish of the medieval elite, made to resemble the color of oranges with an egg yolk glaze. It was listed as pome dorreng on the coronation menu for Henry IV of England.

English kings and nobles bought spices on a grand scale. The Countess of Leicester, daughter of King John, purchased large amounts of cinnamon. King Edward I ordered large quantities of pepper and ginger, and of sugar, which was then an expensive imported luxury.

Guillaume Tirel, known as Taillevent, began as a kitchen boy in 1326 and became chief cook to Charles V of France in 1364. His career lasted sixty-six years. His tombstone shows him in armor, holding a shield with three cooking pots, called marmites.

A French beer described in the 14th century cookbook Le Menagier de Paris was called godale, most likely borrowed from the English 'good ale'. It was made from barley and spelt, without hops. This may reflect the Norman Conquest and nobles traveling between France and England.

At the Stratford guild of the Holy Cross feast in the 15th century, 165 geese and 163 pullets were purchased, most from peasant farmers, because raising poultry was not a common feature of manor houses. Large amounts of wheat were bought to bake bread, and ale was brewed from purchased malt.

Poume d'oranges appears in Anglo-Norman manuscripts, which points to the influence of Arab cuisine on European cooking. This is most likely because the Normans conquered Sicily in the 11th century, after it had been dominated by Arabs for several centuries.

art.text: Gothic architecture was born in the Île-de-France and Picardy regions of northern France. The Abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris is considered the first Gothic building, with its choir reconstructed between 1140 and 1144. The style was sometimes called opus Francigenum, meaning 'French work'.

French Gothic cathedrals such as Notre-Dame, Reims, Chartres and Amiens are known for their height. Rib vaults and flying buttresses spread the weight of the stone to supports on the outside. This allowed unprecedented height and volume, and larger windows that fill the buildings with light.

England's medieval cathedrals date from roughly 1040 to 1540 and number twenty-six buildings. They are a major part of the country's artistic heritage and among the most significant material symbols of Christianity. Each serves as the central church of a diocese and houses a bishop's throne.
art.source_title: Architecture of the medieval cathedrals of England

art.text: Gothic art and architecture formed a medieval movement that began in France and lasted about three hundred years. Its main art media were sculpture, panel painting, stained glass, fresco and illuminated manuscript. By the late fourteenth century it had evolved into a more secular and natural style called International Gothic.

Sens Cathedral, begun between 1135 and 1140 and consecrated in 1160, was the first cathedral built in the new Gothic style. It had a Gothic choir, six-part rib vaults and flying buttresses. Senlis Cathedral and Notre-Dame in Paris, both begun in 1160, soon followed it.

Norwich Cathedral was built between 1096 and 1536 and keeps most of its original Norman stone structure. Between 1416 and 1472 it was vaulted in a spectacular manner, with hundreds of ornately carved, painted and gilded bosses. It also has the finest Norman tower in England, topped by a 15th-century spire.
art.source_title: Architecture of the medieval cathedrals of England

art.text: Romanesque art in France was marked by a renewed interest in Roman construction techniques. The twelfth-century capitals in the cloister of Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert use an acanthus-leaf motif and decorative drill holes, both common on Roman monuments. Normandy saw a large building campaign, including at Bayeux and Mont-Saint-Michel.
William of Sens is believed to have worked on Sens Cathedral. He later traveled to England, where he became the architect who reconstructed the choir of Canterbury Cathedral in the Gothic style.

Worcester Cathedral's nave was built and rebuilt piecemeal by several architects between 1170 and 1374. Some bays form a unique and decorative transition between Norman and Gothic. John Clyve's masterpiece was the central tower of 1374, which originally supported a timber, lead-covered spire that is now gone.
art.source_title: Architecture of the medieval cathedrals of England

art.text: Rib vaults appeared in Durham Cathedral (1093 to 1133) and in Lessay Abbey in Normandy (1098) before Gothic proper. Even so, the first fully Gothic buildings are considered to be the Abbey of Saint-Denis and Sens Cathedral, which systematically combined rib vaulting, buttresses and pointed arches.

The earliest part of Worcester Cathedral is its multi-columned Norman crypt with cushion capitals, from the monastic church begun by St Wulfstan in 1084. The circular chapter house of 1120 was made octagonal on the outside when its walls were reinforced in the 14th century. The last important addition was Prince Arthur's Chantry Chapel, built in 1502 to 1504.
art.source_title: Architecture of the medieval cathedrals of England

art.text: In 1494 Charles VIII led an army into Italy and found the new architecture of the Italian Renaissance far superior to his medieval palace in Amboise. Though forced to retreat, he took home twenty-two skilled Italian craftsmen, including Fra Giocondo and Domenico da Cortona, whom he assigned to remake his château at Amboise.

war.text: The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between the Norman-French army of William, Duke of Normandy, and an English army under King Harold Godwinson. It lasted from about 9 am to dusk, and some historians estimate that 2,000 invaders died along with about twice that number of Englishmen. It was a decisive Norman victory and began the Norman Conquest of England.

The Hundred Years' War lasted from 1337 to 1453 and was fought between England and France, with a civil war inside France as well. Five generations of kings from two rival dynasties fought for the throne of France, then the wealthiest and most populous kingdom in Western Europe.

Charles VII, who reigned from 1422 to 1461, established the first French standing army, the Compagnies d'ordonnance. After the defeats at Poitiers and Agincourt showed that armoured knights could not stand alone, he defeated the Plantagenets at Formigny in 1450 using cannons.

Harold Godwinson faced three invasions in 1066. Harald Hardrada and Tostig beat a hastily gathered English army at Fulford on 20 September, but Harold defeated them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, where Harald Hardrada and Tostig were killed. The Norwegians suffered such great losses that only 24 of the original 300 ships were needed to carry away the survivors. William then landed at Pevensey on 28 September, and Harold, whose army was left battered and weakened, was forced to march south swiftly.

The Hundred Years' War is commonly divided into three phases separated by truces: the Edwardian War (1337-1360), the Caroline War (1369-1389), and the Lancastrian War (1415-1453). It was an intermittent conflict, frequently interrupted by external factors such as the Black Death, a deadly plague that spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351. In France 6 to 12 million people died, 30-60% of the population, and in England roughly 2-3 million died.

After the humiliating defeats of Poitiers in 1356 and Agincourt in 1415, the French nobility realised they could not stand just as armoured knights without an organised army. Charles VII then established the first French standing army, the Compagnies d'ordonnance.

The Battle of Castillon took place on 17 July 1453 in Gascony and was the first major European battle won through the extensive use of field artillery. The English commander John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, attacked a strongly fortified French encampment, where the French guns obliterated the advancing soldiers, each shot reportedly killing six men at a time. Talbot's reinforcements kept arriving only to suffer the same fate in turn, and the battle ended in an English rout in which both Talbot and his son were killed.

Resistance to the Normans continued for years after Hastings. William faced rebellions in Exeter in late 1067 and an uprising in Northumbria in 1068, and in 1069 more Northumbrian rebels, an invading Danish fleet and risings in the south and west. He ruthlessly put down the risings, culminating in the Harrying of the North in late 1069 and early 1070, which devastated parts of northern England. A further rebellion in 1070 by Hereward the Wake was also defeated by the king, at Ely.

Charles VII defeated the Plantagenets at Patay in 1429 and again at Formigny in 1450, where he used cannons. The Battle of Castillon in 1453 was regarded as the last engagement of the war, yet Calais and the Channel Islands remained ruled by the Plantagenets.

John Talbot mistakenly believed the enemy was retreating, when the dust cloud was in fact camp followers leaving before the battle, and attacked with a relatively small advance force without waiting for reinforcements. He then refused to withdraw even after realising the strength of the French position, and ordered his men to keep fighting while outnumbered. The battle ended in an English rout, and Talbot was killed. There is some debate over the circumstances, but it appears his horse was killed by a cannon shot and, with its mass pinning him down, a French archer killed him with an axe.

After Castillon, the English lost nearly all their holdings in France, especially Gascony, which the Plantagenet kings had held for three centuries. Calais remained the last English possession on the mainland until it was lost in 1558.

Some have speculated that news of the defeat at Castillon led to the mental collapse of Henry VI of England in late 1453. His loss of mental capacity led to the outbreak of the Wars of the Roses in England.

Henry I invaded the Duchy of Normandy in 1105 and 1106, finally defeating his elder brother Robert at the Battle of Tinchebray. Henry kept Robert imprisoned for the rest of his life, and after victory at Brémule a favourable peace was agreed with Louis VI of France in 1120.
war.source_title: England in the High Middle Ages

literature.text: Rhyming stories of the Old French Crusade cycle were popular with medieval audiences in Northern France, Occitania and Iberia. From the late 12th century, tales of the sieges of Antioch and Jerusalem described battles, suffering, and Saracen plunder, including silks, gold and masterfully embroidered and woven tents.

Beginning in the 11th century, literature written in medieval French was one of the oldest vernacular (non-Latin) literatures in western Europe. It became a key source of literary themes across the continent during the Middle Ages.

The scholar Charles Homer Haskins coined the phrase "Renaissance of the 12th century" for the conditions in France around the year 1100. For the next hundred years, writers, jongleurs, clercs and poets produced a profusion of remarkable creative works in all genres.

The Matter of Britain is the body of medieval literature and legend tied to Great Britain and Brittany, especially King Arthur. Its pseudo-chronicle and chivalric romance works, in prose and verse, flourished from the 12th to the 16th century.

After the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, French became the standard language of courts, parliament and polite society. Geoffrey Chaucer, author of The Canterbury Tales, helped establish the legitimacy of Middle English at a time when French and Latin were still the dominant literary languages in England.

Medieval European literature often used "Saracen" as both an ethnic and a religious marker. Some works equated Saracens with Muslims in general and described them as dark-skinned, as in the romance The King of Tars. The 11th-century Old French Song of Roland calls their black skin their only exotic feature.

Around a hundred verse romances survive from the period 1150 to 1220. From around 1200 on, romances were increasingly written in prose, and many earlier verse romances were adapted into prose versions.

The three "matters" of medieval storytelling were first described in the 12th century by the French poet Jean Bodel. His epic Chanson des Saisnes, or "Song of the Saxons", names the Matter of France, about Charlemagne and his companions, alongside the Matter of Britain and the Matter of Rome.

Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote the 12th-century Historia Regum Britanniae, a central part of the Matter of Britain. Its supposedly historical Arthurian content, carried on by successors such as Wace, along with Welsh and Breton tales like the Mabinogion, became the foundation for Arthurian romances.

Layamon's Brut adapted the Norman-French of Wace to produce the first English-language work presenting the legends of King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table. It was also the first historiography written in English since the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

The Ormulum was written between about 1150 and 1180. It highlighted for the first time the blending of Old English and Anglo-Norman elements in English, marking the beginning of the Middle English period.

The Roman de Fauvel, dated to 1310 and 1314, is a satire on abuses in the medieval church. It is filled with motets, lais, rondeaux and other new secular forms of poetry and music, including several pieces by Philippe de Vitry, who coined the expression Ars nova.

The prose satire Les XV joies de mariage, first published in 1480 to 1490, is a riotous critique of wives. It also gives important insight into the economic and social life of a married household in the 15th century. It has been attributed variously to Antoine de la Sale, Gilles Bellemère and many others.

Thomas Malory's 15th-century compilation Le Morte d'Arthur established an English-language quasi-canon of the Arthurian romance tradition, based on the French prose cycles and some other works. The 19th-century Romanticist revival brought the legend back primarily in the form of Malory's telling.

science.text: After the Renaissance of the 12th century, medieval Europe saw a radical change in the rate of new inventions. The period brought gunpowder, vertical windmills, spectacles, mechanical clocks, and greatly improved water mills. Three-field crop rotation also improved agriculture in general.

William Caxton and Wynkyn de Worde began using the printing press in England during the late 15th century. Separately, the introduction of hopped beer had transformed the brewing industry in the 14th century.

By the 13th century, England was home to approximately 300 leper hospitals, which served as both medical facilities and religious communities. Residents lived by strict routines of prayer and isolation, reflecting a societal fear of leprosy as a contagious and divinely ordained affliction. Notable examples included St. Mary Magdalen Hospital in Winchester and St. Leonard's Hospital in York, and most were founded between the 11th and 13th centuries as acts of charity.

By the time of the Domesday Book, most large villages had turnable mills, around 6,500 in England alone. Water power spread from agriculture to sawmills for timber and stone. It was also used in mining to raise ore from shafts, crush ore, and power bellows.
Windmills began to be built in England in the late 12th century and slowly became more common. Water-powered fulling mills and powered hammers first appeared in the 12th century as well.

Plate armour covered the entire body, and parts of it such as poleyns for the knees and couters for the elbows were in use as early as 1250. The first complete full suit without any textiles appeared around 1410 to 1430. Advances in metal working such as the blast furnace and new carburizing techniques made it nearly impenetrable.

Watermills to grind grain existed for most of the Anglo-Saxon period, using horizontal designs. From the 12th century many more were built, which ended the use of hand mills. The older horizontal mills were gradually replaced by a new vertical mill design.

Water power was harnessed to assist in smelting in England by the 14th century. The first English blast furnace opened in 1496. By the end of the Middle Ages, horse-powered pumps had also been installed in English mines.

The wheelbarrow proved useful in building construction, mining and agriculture. Literary evidence for its use appears in north-western Europe between 1170 and 1250. The first depiction is in a drawing by Matthew Paris in the mid-13th century.

The Third Lateran Council in 1179 and the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 issued decrees calling for separate living spaces for lepers, to prevent what they called moral and physical contamination. Some hospitals even built chapels so that lepers could attend services while physically separated from non-leprous congregants. The Church was instrumental in setting formal policies on the segregation and care of lepers.

The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 diverted resources and public attention in England away from leprosy toward the plague, and is estimated to have killed between 30% and 50% of the English population. About 20% of mortality occurred among clergy, who often tended the sick and caught the diseases themselves. Many nobles and clergy who had supported leper hospitals died, donations dropped drastically, and the loss of monks, priests and caregivers left many hospitals without enough staff, often leading to their closure or repurposing.

politics.text: From 1028 to 1035, Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway together. This North Sea Empire made him the most powerful ruler in western Europe after the Holy Roman Emperor. Its parts were connected only by the sea.

When Charles IV of France died in 1328 without male heirs, the main Capetian line ended. Under Salic law the crown could not pass through a woman, even though Philip IV's daughter Isabella had a son, Edward III of England. The throne went to Philip VI, and this helped lead to the Hundred Years' War of 1337-1453.

King John's behaviour led to rebellions that weakened Angevin control on the continent. After capturing the rebel leadership at the Battle of Mirebeau, John's nephew Arthur was murdered, rumoured to have been done by John's own hands, and Arthur's Eleanor spent the rest of her life in captivity. John's behaviour drove numerous French barons to side with Philip, and John's defeats then weakened his position in England, leading the barons to rebel and produce Magna Carta, which limited royal power. His death in 1216 marked the end of the Angevin period.
politics.source_title: England in the High Middle Ages

politics.text: Philip II was the first king to call himself rex Francie, 'King of France', in 1190, and did so officially from 1204. Before that, the French ruler had been styled rex Francorum, 'king of the Franks'. In 1204 the Duchy of Normandy was also absorbed by the French crown.

Edward I, who inherited the throne in 1272, restored royal authority and gained control of Wales and most of Scotland. His son Edward II was defeated at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314 and lost control of Scotland. Edward II was deposed in a coup and is generally believed to have been murdered at Berkeley Castle by having a red-hot poker thrust into his bowels. In 1330 his son Edward III took control of the kingdom.
politics.source_title: England in the Late Middle Ages

politics.text: In 1415 Henry V of England won a shattering victory at Agincourt against a France bitterly divided between Armagnac and Burgundian factions. Under the 1420 Treaty of Troyes his son Henry VI was recognised as king in Paris. Valois rule was reduced to the lands south of the Loire Valley.

In 1429 Joan of Arc raised the siege of Orléans and had Charles VII crowned at Reims, an important French propaganda victory. English efforts were hampered by power struggles between Bedford, his brother Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, and their uncle Cardinal Beaufort.

Reconciliation in 1435 between Charles VII and Philippe the Good, Duke of Burgundy, removed the greatest obstacle to French recovery. France then recaptured Paris in 1436, Normandy in 1450 and Guienne in 1453. England was left with only a small area around Calais.

When William the Conqueror died in 1087, his Norman lands went to Robert Curthose and his English lands to William Rufus. Nobles holding land on both sides of the Channel rebelled for Robert in 1088 under Bishop Odo of Bayeux. William Rufus won over the English lords with silver and promises of better government, then invaded Normandy in 1091.
politics.source_title: England in the High Middle Ages

politics.text: Normandy was absorbed by the French crown in 1204, followed by Toulouse in 1271 and Champagne in 1284. In 1297 three new peerages were created to replace the lost ones: Artois, Anjou and Brittany. The number of lay peerages reached 26 in 1400.

Between 1429 and 1453 the French drove the English out of France. The Hundred Years' War was finally ended by the Treaty of Picquigny in 1475, when Edward IV agreed not to pursue his claim further. English and later British monarchs kept the title of King or Queen of France until 1801.

The Valois claim to the French throne rested on a precedent from 1316 that excluded females such as Joan II of Navarre. It also excluded male descendants through the female line, such as Edward III of England. The rule was only later attributed retroactively to the Merovingian Salic law.

philosophy.text: French philosophy begins in the medieval period with authors writing in Latin. That language was brought by the Romanization of Gaul and Gallo-Roman culture.

Scholasticism was a method of learning more than a philosophy or a theology. It relied on dialectical reasoning to extend knowledge by inference and to resolve contradictions, and it aimed to reconcile classical philosophy, especially Aristotelian logic, with Catholic Christianity.

Scholasticism emerged within monastic schools that rediscovered the collected works of Aristotle. These schools became the basis of the earliest European medieval universities. The movement flourished in Italy, France, Portugal, Spain and England.

Medieval philosophy was defined partly by rediscovering the ancient culture of Greece and Rome, and partly by the need to address theological problems. Thinkers tried to integrate sacred doctrine with secular learning. Understanding God was the focal point of study for Jewish, Christian and Muslim philosophers and theologians.

Scholasticism had four primary founders. Johannes Scotus Eriugena was one, and the other three were the 11th-century archbishops Lanfranc and Anselm of Canterbury in England and Peter Abelard in France.

The high medieval or scholastic period is generally agreed to begin with Saint Anselm of Canterbury, who lived from 1033 to 1109. He is famous as the originator of the ontological argument for the existence of God.

Anselm of Canterbury was born in 1033 in Aosta. In his mid-twenties he entered the Benedictine school at Bec in Normandy, where he studied under Lanfranc. He succeeded Lanfranc as prior in 1063 and was consecrated abbot in 1078.

William of Moerbeke's translations and editions of Greek philosophical texts in the middle of the thirteenth century gave a clearer picture of Aristotle than the Arabic versions had. Those earlier versions had distorted the relation between Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy. Moerbeke's work formed the basis of the major commentaries that followed.

In the 1380s, several challenges to the traditional theology of the Church emerged in England, resulting from the teachings of John Wycliffe. After his death in 1384 a loose movement that included many gentry pursued his ideas, and the authorities rapidly condemned it as "Lollardy", using the powers of both church and state against it. In 1414 Sir John Oldcastle, a suspected Lollard, escaped from imprisonment, prompting a planned rising in London. The authorities arrested the conspirators, and a further round of political trials and persecutions followed. Oldcastle was captured and executed in 1417.

Anselm of Canterbury held the office of Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109. Besides the ontological argument he originated the satisfaction theory of atonement. His works count as philosophical as well as theological because they render Christian tenets, traditionally taken as revealed truth, into a rational system.
Medieval philosophy of mind was based on Aristotle's De Anima, another work discovered in the Latin West in the twelfth century. It was regarded as a branch of the philosophy of nature.
Gerard of Siena (c. 1295 – d. 1336) was a Tuscan student of Giles of Rome at the University of Paris. He opposed usury and lectured on Peter Lombard's Sentences.

culture.text: By 1215, there were over 600 monastic communities in England. Later in the twelfth century the Cistercians arrived, building houses with a more austere reading of the monastic rules, including the great abbeys of Rievaulx and Fountains.

Pilgrimage was a popular religious practice throughout the Middle Ages in England. Taking part in the Crusades was also seen as a form of pilgrimage, and England played a prominent part in the Second, Third and Fifth Crusades.

By the 13th century, England was home to approximately 300 leper hospitals. They were both medical facilities and religious communities, and residents followed strict routines of prayer and isolation. This reflected a societal fear of leprosy as a contagious and divinely ordained affliction, and the hospitals physically isolated the afflicted from the general population.

Teaching is evidenced at the University of Oxford as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. The University of Cambridge, founded in 1209, received a royal charter from Henry III in 1231.

Medieval English schools taught Latin grammar to the sons of the aristocracy who were destined for the priesthood or monastic work. Oxford and Cambridge were both established in affiliation with the church, to further train Catholic clergy.

Hopped beer transformed the English brewing industry in the 14th century. By the 15th century, stoneware pots had largely replaced wooden plates and bowls, after glazed pottery became widespread in the 12th and 13th centuries.

The Hospital of St. Mary Magdalen in Winchester was one of the earliest recorded leper hospitals in England, founded in the late 11th or early 12th century. Excavations there revealed remains consistent with a central chapel, dormitories and infirmary spaces, and a large burial site. The skeletons showed bone lesions, facial deformities and limb damage consistent with advanced leprosy.
Apprenticeship was the main way for English youths to enter practical occupations. Guilds controlled many trades and used apprenticeships to control entry.

The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 hastened the decline of leper hospitals in England, as public concern turned to other diseases. It is estimated to have killed between 30% and 50% of England's population, and about 20% of mortality occurred among clergy, who often tended the sick and caught the diseases themselves. With so many donors and caregivers dead, donations fell drastically and many leper hospitals could not keep running.
